def token_game(n, edges, tokens):
    """Determine the outcome of a multi-token game on a directed graph.

    The graph has n vertices numbered 0..n-1 and a list of directed edges
    (u, v), each meaning a move from u to v is allowed.  Tokens are placed
    on vertices (several tokens may occupy the same vertex).  Two players
    alternate turns; on each turn the current player chooses ONE token and
    moves it along one outgoing edge of the vertex it stands on.  Any token
    may be chosen on any turn, including the same token repeatedly.  A
    player who cannot move (every token stands on a vertex with no outgoing
    edge) loses.  The graph may contain cycles, so play can continue
    forever; infinite play is a draw.

    Both players play optimally: each prefers winning to drawing, and
    drawing to losing.

    Input domain:
      n      -- int, 1 <= n <= 50
      edges  -- list of distinct pairs (u, v) with 0 <= u, v < n and
                u != v (no self-loops, no duplicate edges)
      tokens -- list of 1 to 50 ints, each in 0..n-1 (repeats allowed):
                the starting vertices of the tokens

    Returns exactly one of the strings:
      'FIRST'  -- the player who moves first can force a win
      'SECOND' -- the second player can force a win
      'DRAW'   -- neither player can force a win, but each can avoid
                  losing (play lasts forever under optimal play)

    Note: the number of distinct token configurations can exceed 10**28,
    so any search over positions of the full game is hopeless.  Also, a
    token being able to reach a cycle does not by itself make the game a
    draw.

    >>> token_game(3, [(0, 1), (1, 2)], [0])
    'SECOND'
    >>> token_game(2, [(0, 1), (1, 0)], [0])
    'DRAW'
    >>> token_game(4, [(0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 0), (2, 3)], [2])
    'FIRST'
    >>> token_game(4, [(0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 0), (2, 3)], [2, 2])
    'DRAW'
    """
